newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's ex-premier Gonzalez roars in opposition. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Spain's ex-premier Gonzalez roars in opposition. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: Former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez returned to Spain's political scene with a roar on Monday, blasting the ruling Popular Party (PP) in his first news conference since he lost power four months ago.

Gonzalez, who governed Spain for 13 years until he lost power in May following elections in March (corrects from "lost elections in May"), said he was ready to take up his role as head of the opposition Socialists.
The opposition had seemed rudderless as Gonzalez took long holidays, toured in South America and immersed himself in international Socialist affairs.

The veteran leader blasted the new conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, saying: "I have the impression that they don't know they are in government. It's about time they realised it."
Gonzalez attacked PP reversals on health care, pensions and regional financing as he marked out his turf as opposition leader in what he called his first official day.
But he approved of the government's decision to keep military intelligence files on a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque rebels secret, calling it a "secure and responsible" act.
The former prime minister's prolonged absence from public life had become something of joke.

"If you want to put a date on it, take today as the end of my period of decompression," he said. "If a period of discretion is considered prudent in order that the government may start to take the reins of the country, they say you are on holiday."

The daily El Pais criticised the former leader on Monday for failing to question PP moves and urged him to influence the 1997 budget, which needs to be strict if Spain is to join a single European currency -- a goal shared by the Socialists.

"Nine million voters deposited a confidence in him that has until now been undermined," it said. "The common Maastricht goal doesn't exclude different ways of reaching those objectives by a conservative government and a progressive opposition."

Gonzalez, who is still under Supreme Court scrutiny for alleged involvement in the "dirty war", said he was now ready to start his opposition role and swept aside PP accusations that he lacked moral authority.

"This is not an obstacle to my political life," Gonzalez said, referring to the pending Supreme Court decision on whether he should be questioned or charged in relation with the 27 murders carried out by death squads between 1983 and 1987.

Former interior minister Jose Barrionuevo and other party officials have been indicted on charges the Socialist government of the time set up and financed the campaign by security forces and hired gunmen against suspected Basque separatists.

Courts investigating the death squads have been denied access to the secret files by both administrations, spurring the communist-led United Left (IU) coalition to accuse the PP of conspiring with the Socialists to cover up the crimes.
News reports on Monday said the Supreme Court actually possessed the files, which were confiscated when former spy Colonel Juan Alberto Perote was arrested, but not in a legally usable form.

Perote, who stole the files when he left the military intelligence service, was so desperate to keep certain documents out of court hands that he reportedly tried to eat them as a judge searched his cell.
His cellmate was also caught trying to hide some of the documents in the prison library stacks.
While the PP and the Socialists agree the "dirty war" papers should remain secret, they are still divided on whether they should play a role in Spanish politics.

"A person who has left the prestige of the premiership at the feet of the Supreme Court doesn't have moral or political authority," Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos said in an attack on Gonzalez at the weekend.
